terms.grammar: adjective; comparative stultior; as a noun, stultus, a fool
evidence: Cic. Sen. 67: quis est tam stultus …?
terms.comment: The everyday word, in comedy and in Cicero alike, for a person, an act or an idea; stultē, stupidly; stultitia, stupidity.

evidence: Plaut. Aul. 3.2.1: quid, stolide, clāmās? (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Stronger than stultus: dense, slow to take anything in; of things, inert. Common in comedy as an insult, and in Livy.

evidence: Ter. Eun. 5.9.49: fatuus est, īnsulsus (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Witless, a fool; of food, insipid (Mart. 13.13).

evidence: Cic. Par. 37: Echiōnis tabula tē stupidum dētinet (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Not the everyday word for stupid, though English takes it from here: first struck dumb, rapt, gaping at a picture or a show, and only then dull or stupid (Zopyrus called Socrates stupidum et bardum, Cic. Fat. 10).
Lewis & Short: very rare. Traupman gives it for the colloquial “jerk”.

terms.gloss: act foolishly, make a fool of oneself

terms.comment: Not found in Lewis & Short or the loci collections.

evidence: Cic. Fin. 2.76: nōs bārōnēs stupēmus (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Four times in Cicero, rare elsewhere (Lewis & Short).

phrases.latin: quis est tam stultus, quamvīs sit adulēscēns, cui sit explōrātum sē ad vesperum esse vīctūrum?
phrases.english: who is so foolish, however young, as to be sure he will live till evening?
what a difference between a man of sense and a fool!

phrases.latin: Taciturnitās stultō hominī prō sapientiā est.
phrases.english: for a fool, silence passes for wisdom
